title: The Characteristic of a Field
---

Every ring receives a distinguished homomorphism from the integers. For a field, its kernel is an important invariant.

For an element $a$ of a ring and $n \in \ZZ$, we write $n \cdot a$ for the $n$-th multiple of $a$ in the additive group: $n \cdot a = a + \cdots + a$ ($n$ terms) for $n > 0$, $0 \cdot a = 0$, and $n \cdot a = -((-n) \cdot a)$ for $n < 0$. This is the additive version of the powers $a^n$ in a group from Chapter 2, so $(m + n) \cdot a = m \cdot a + n \cdot a$ and $m \cdot (n \cdot a) = (mn) \cdot a$. Distributivity and Proposition [4.1.3](/notes/math-55a/4-1-rings-and-fields#proposition-4-1-3) give $(n \cdot a)b = n \cdot (ab)$.

:::proposition{4.4.1} The homomorphism from $\ZZ$
For any ring $R$ there is a unique ring homomorphism $\varphi : \ZZ \to R$, namely $\varphi(n) = n \cdot 1_R$.
:::

:::proof
Uniqueness: a ring homomorphism $\varphi$ is in particular a homomorphism of additive groups with $\varphi(1) = 1_R$. Since $1$ generates $(\ZZ, +)$, it is determined by this value: $\varphi(n) = n \cdot \varphi(1) = n \cdot 1_R$.

Existence: define $\varphi(n) = n \cdot 1_R$. Then $\varphi(m + n) = \varphi(m) + \varphi(n)$ and $\varphi(1) = 1_R$. Finally, $$\varphi(m)\varphi(n) = (m \cdot 1_R)(n \cdot 1_R) = m \cdot \big(1_R (n \cdot 1_R)\big) = m \cdot (n \cdot 1_R) = (mn) \cdot 1_R = \varphi(mn).$$
:::

Now let $k$ be a field and $\varphi : \ZZ \to k$ this homomorphism. Its kernel is a subgroup of $\ZZ$, hence equal to $n\ZZ$ for a unique $n \geq 0$ (Theorem [2.4.5](/notes/math-55a/2-4-subgroups#theorem-2-4-5)).

:::proposition{4.4.2} The kernel is zero or prime
The kernel of $\varphi : \ZZ \to k$ is $n\ZZ$ where either $n = 0$ or $n = p$ is prime.
:::

:::proof
We have $n \neq 1$, since $\varphi(1) = 1_k \neq 0$. Suppose $n > 1$ is not prime, so $n = ab$ with $1 < a, b < n$. Then $$\varphi(a)\varphi(b) = \varphi(ab) = \varphi(n) = 0,$$ and since a field has no zero divisors, $\varphi(a) = 0$ or $\varphi(b) = 0$. That is, $a \in n\ZZ$ or $b \in n\ZZ$, which is impossible for $0 < a, b < n$. Hence if $n > 0$, then $n$ is prime.
:::

:::definition{4.4.3} Characteristic
The ***characteristic*** of a field $k$, denoted $\mathrm{char}(k)$, is

- $0$ if $\ker\varphi = \{0\}$, i.e., $\varphi : \ZZ \to k$ is injective;
- $p$ if $\ker \varphi = p\ZZ$ for a prime $p$.

Equivalently, $\mathrm{char}(k) = p > 0$ means that $\underbrace{1_k + 1_k + \cdots + 1_k}_{p \text{ terms}} = 0_k$ and $p$ is the smallest positive integer with this property, while $\mathrm{char}(k) = 0$ means that $n \cdot 1_k \neq 0$ for every $n \geq 1$.
:::

In a field of characteristic $p$, we have $p \cdot a = (p \cdot 1)a = 0$ for every $a$. In characteristic $2$ in particular, $1 + 1 = 0$, that is, $-1 = 1$.

:::example{4.4.4}
- $\mathrm{char}(\QQ) = \mathrm{char}(\RR) = \mathrm{char}(\CC) = 0$: the map $\ZZ \to \QQ$ is the inclusion.
- $\mathrm{char}(\FF_p) = p$ for every prime $p$: $p \cdot 1 = 0$ in $\ZZ/p$, while $n \cdot 1 = n \neq 0$ for $0 < n < p$.
- $\mathrm{char}(k(x)) = \mathrm{char}(k(\!(x)\!)) = \mathrm{char}(k)$: these fields contain $k$ as a subfield, so the homomorphism from $\ZZ$ to either of them is $\ZZ \to k$ followed by the inclusion, and has the same kernel.
:::

:::note
The field $\FF_p = \ZZ/p$ is the ***prime field*** of characteristic $p$. Every field $k$ of characteristic $p$ contains a copy of $\FF_p$: since $a \cdot 1_k = b \cdot 1_k$ exactly when $p$ divides $a - b$, the map $\FF_p \to k$, $a \mapsto a \cdot 1_k$, is an injective ring homomorphism. Every field of characteristic $0$ contains a copy of $\QQ$, via $m/n \mapsto (m \cdot 1_k)(n \cdot 1_k)^{-1}$. Thus $\FF_p$ and $\QQ$ are the smallest fields of their characteristics.
:::

:::theorem{4.4.5} Existence and uniqueness of finite fields
For every prime $p$ and every $n \geq 1$, there exists a field with exactly $p^n$ elements, unique up to isomorphism, denoted $\FF_{p^n}$ or $\mathrm{GF}(p^n)$. Every finite field is of this form.
:::

:::note
We do not prove this theorem here. The field $\FF_{p^n}$ can be constructed as a splitting field of $x^{p^n} - x$ over $\FF_p$ (splitting fields are discussed in Chapter 17). There are also infinite fields of characteristic $p$, for example the field of rational functions $\FF_p(x)$ and the field of Laurent series $\FF_p(\!(x)\!)$.
:::
